entry.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
entry.content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

[Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 (v1), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)]

Title:Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own WeightsView PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training. entry.title: I'm Peter Roberts, immigration attorney who does work for YC and startups. AMA
Google Workers Tell Their Employer Not to Punish Schools That Don't Want AI
entry.content:
Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year.

Google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools.

As I wrote last week after attending a rally in New York City:

Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.

Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.

That day, protests took place in six other cities—Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.

School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini.

Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines.

“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union, which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”

“It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search.

A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its specific demands.

AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line,” the Google engineer said.

Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to Mother Jones that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”

That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.

“If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked.

Google has been contacted for comment.

entry.title: Running two PSP emulators on one Switch 2 and sharing one via GameShare
entry.content:
This branch experiments with a separate PPSSPP guest running on the host Switch 2 and streamed to a stock GameShare client. It is not a mirrored controller or a second PSP controller in the host emulator. Compilation and host tests do not establish console operation or acceptable two-game performance.

The working single-instance checkpoint is switch2-single-instance-working (commit 1c3b38a). Its exact tested NRO, package and matching debug ELF remain under dist-switch2/checkpoints/switch2-single-instance-working/.

sh Tools/build-switch2-gameshare.sh python3 Tools/deploy-switch2.py 192.168.1.182 --experimental-gameshare

Open FTPD for the second command. A successful transfer is accepted without a validation download. The experiment installs as PPSSPP GameShare, at sdmc:/switch/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare.nro. It leaves the working ppsspp-switch2 NRO and its settings/saves in place. The normal Tools/build-switch2.sh selects GameShare OFF. Both builds reuse the build cache, but packaging rejects mismatched native/experimental modes.

Launch through the same GameShare-capable native title override used for the Moonlight SDK example. A generic title override is not known to grant the required GameShare context. If another title locks profile switching, the SDK uses the Nintendo profile selected for that launch when available. The host log distinguishes a missing launch profile from a later StreamPlay or matchmaking error. Choose GameShare (experimental) in the host's main or pause menu, then join from the client's system GameShare screen. The client should see its own PPSSPP menu, with a guest-only startup message, and browse sdmc:/switch/ppsspp-switch2/games. Both browsers can access SD-card games; no game files are copied into the package.

Choose the same GameShare action to stop sharing. The guest pauses between sessions, retaining its independent emulator state. Exiting the guest's PPSSPP ends that guest instance; restart the application before creating another. Exit the host normally when done. If a real cleanup failure reports retained resources, close the entire hosting title from HOME, rather than returning to hbmenu. The SDK explicitly requires this for uncertain native ownership.

The build links a second PPSSPP frontend/core into a relocatable object and renames every defined core-owned global symbol and ELF COMDAT group signature. Only eight plain-data C entry points are exported. The audit requires distinct Config, memory-base and core-state symbols; the host also compares their runtime addresses before starting. SDK/OS/C++ runtime entry points remain shared. The two emulators have independent core, UI, filesystem state, JIT registries, Vulkan contexts and settings/memory-stick directories. They share one OS process, so a fatal error in either copy can still affect the entire app.

The host keeps its 1920x1080 output and 120 Hz request. The guest uses PPSSPP's existing offscreen Vulkan path at 1280x720 with a 60 fps presentation target. A readback callback transfers completed RGBA frames to a latest-frame mailbox; a dedicated presenter uploads them to a separate native VI2 guest layer. This first route adds CPU readback/swizzle cost; zero-copy is not claimed.

The GameShare SDK is vendored from Moonlight-Switch's research worktree. Switch/GameShare/sdk-provenance.json records the source revision and file hashes. Its MIT license and per-file ISC notices are retained. The SDK's pinned CPU-console uploader is disabled. The guest renderer borrows the statically linked OunceVK driver's GSV main and worker sessions and uses its registered VM. It owns the guest image backing, registrations and client. The adapter tracks the driver's occupied slots at the libounce call boundary and reserves a free slot for guest range retirement. Each GameShare session reuses the reserved slot's completion event, which closes with the Vulkan driver's GPU. It does not access OunceVK's internal structs. Retire the guest images before Vulkan teardown. Coexistence and reuse on hardware still require qualification.

The SDK owns matchmaking, native hosting, controller reads and the separate VI2 display/layer. Renderer retirement runs before native Finalize; layer closure runs afterwards. Uncertain presentation or release/retirement failure retains backing and blocks ordinary unload. Guest controls never enter the host emulator. Stale/disconnected snapshots become neutral.

Host settings/saves use ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/config/ppsspp; guest settings/saves use ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/guest/config/ppsspp. The existing working app's memory stick is not reused. Guest native text-entry applets are disabled because their routing to the remote screen is not implemented.

PPSSPP sends the guest emulator's PCM to the native per-guest queue and keeps the host emulator on normal AudOut. See the recovered audio contract. The console test confirmed audible client playback in the direct-audio build.

Start GameShare and join from the client. Open the same game on both screens, then enter its local wireless or Ad Hoc mode. Create a lobby on either console and look for it on the other. If the host had already initialized multiplayer before pairing, restart that game once to select the local route.

While GameShare is hosting, PPSSPP runs its built-in discovery service and aemu_postoffice packet relay on IPv4 loopback ports 27314 and 27315. Both cores use the private route automatically with their existing, independently configured PSP MAC addresses. The guest still runs on the host Switch 2, so game packets stay on that console. The route does not use a public relay, Wi-Fi IP address, or UPnP mapping, and it does not change either core's saved network settings. Stopping GameShare closes the listeners. A game already in a lobby may need to leave and re-enter multiplayer after GameShare is restarted.

The user reported a successful Tekken session in the first loopback build. The subsequent build keeps each core's original MAC address and passed the ten paired desktop tests. That save-preserving version is tagged switch2-gameshare-multiplayer-baseline (commit 0699365). Its NRO, ZIP and debug ELF are in dist-switch2-gameshare/checkpoints/multiplayer-baseline/. The earlier console run used the temporary-MAC build.

Host boot.log, ppsspp.log, native-exit.bin and native-fault.bin live in the experimental app directory. The guest writes guest/ppsspp.log. Native fault/exit records with valid headers are retained as .previous on the next launch. Preserve diagnostics before relaunching after a failure.

python3 Switch/tests/run.py python3 Switch/tests/run_gameshare.py python3 Switch/GameShare/sdk/tests/native/run.py python3 Switch/GameShare/sdk/tests/guest_input/run.py python3 Switch/GameShare/sdk/tests/guest_display/run.py git diff --check

Actual-source sanitizer tests cover native guest-image sector locations, partial creation, successful retirement, retained uncertain presents and release/range timeouts. SDK tests cover native lifecycle/cancellation, controller parsing/freshness and display ownership. They do not simulate the GPU, native title permissions, GameShare radio behavior or console performance. CPU, GPU, threading and shutdown regression risks require console testing; serialized PSP state layouts are unchanged.

The dual-core AArch64 NRO and ZIP built and validated. The symbol audit found 27,173 renamed core-owned symbols and eight guest ABI exports. All 28 SDK native lifecycle scenarios, the input parser/freshness suite and display lifetime suite passed under ASan/UBSan. Six actual-source image-owner scenarios passed (clean, partial create, uncertain present, release timeout, range retirement timeout and unregister failure). Existing JIT publication and dedicated-worker tests also passed.

Host regression suites: 102 C++ unit tests passed; 527 executed single-instance PSP cases and ten paired relay scenarios passed. Eleven paired P2P cases remain unrun for the existing missing 127.0.0.2 host loopback alias, causing the aggregate runner's failure status. No executed regression test failed. Console dual-instance rendering, pairing, guest controls/audio and sustained performance still require physical qualification.

The initial experimental build produced a system error before the PPSSPP menu. Its boot log reached display configuration; native fault/exit records remained empty. The separate working single-instance installation is unchanged. Pairing and the second emulator have not yet been reached on the console.

The SDK bridge is compiled as C++20 separately from the C++17 frontend. Startup checkpoints around Vulkan initialization write startup-stage.bin directly with native flushes. Its four little-endian 64-bit words are magic 0x3254475350505350, stage number, recorder address and system tick. Stages 1–4 cover diagnostics, display configuration, graphics-object construction and error-string construction; stages 10 and 11 bracket InitAPI's initial string assignment. Stages 20 and 21 bracket NativeInit, and 22 precedes window setup. The diagnostic boot marker is comdat-isolation. The native exit recorder also wraps svcBreak (kind 6, reason in the high 32 bits and a readable four-byte detail in the low 32 bits).

The final ELF showed that the linker turned a required host string-constructor call into a no-op. GCC used a local C5 signature for the constructor group. Renaming only global symbols let the guest group retain that signature, causing the linker to discard the host copy. The build now renames and checks all 7,351 guest COMDAT groups in addition to the global symbol audit. Disassembly of the corrected ELF confirms that host startup calls its own string constructor and the guest constructor has a distinct address.

The console opened the corrected build and started a host game. On the first GameShare attempt, VI2 reached the renderer hook, where a second GSV GPU open failed with 0x200F3. The guest emulator independently reached offscreen Vulkan initialization. The revised uploader uses the existing driver session. The host also joins the SDK thread after terminal states before asking if native resources were retained, so a completed thread alone no longer forces a title restart. Confirm pairing, guest frames and stop/restart on hardware.

The shared-session build paired with the client, and the SDK completed cleanup. The client remained black because PPSSPP rejected readback from the guest's offscreen Vulkan presentation before any frame could reach the uploader. Offscreen presentation now declares its transfer-source capability. The copy waits for the color attachment writes and skips frames without an acquired image. A local MoltenVK run cleared three consecutive offscreen frames to different colors and verified every returned RGBA byte. Client presentation and independent input still require a console check.

The console confirmed that the host and client can see and control their own PPSSPP screens. Both emulator audio streams were audible from the host. The console-confirmed NRO, matching ELF and installation receipt are saved under dist-switch2-gameshare/checkpoints/dual-screen-controls/.

The client was silent in separate-display sessions with both AudOut and Audren. The Audren test boot log confirms the application mix used Audren, the guest received frames and SDK cleanup completed. The launcher NRO was restored to the console-confirmed dual-screen build using the saved SD-card copy. The renderer trial is recorded in commit c5a8716.

At the dual-screen checkpoint, both games played through the host. The SDK exposed an application-wide mirroring flag and device-volume configuration.

The shipped SDK exports a separate PCM writer and per-guest queue counters. The reusable Moonlight SDK and its PPSSPP copy now expose a PCM callback. Tests of the native worker cover the recovered command layout, the unwritten tail after a partial write, and a failed audio command that leaves video and input running.

On November 19, 2026, the console test confirmed sound on the GameShare client. The working build is tagged switch2-gameshare-guest-audio-working (commit 50cd977). The exact installed NRO, SD-card package, matching ELF, SDK archive and build records are saved under dist-switch2-gameshare/checkpoints/guest-audio-working/. For a console rollback, reinstall that NRO as /switch/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare.nro.

entry.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
entry.content:
Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:

Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions, which is formalized in Lean here. Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization. Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof. Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). (UPDATE: the moderators of the Lean thread are now focusing the discussion on the Lean-related aspects of the proof only.) I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task.

See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.

entry.title: Vibecoding an inference chip
entry.content:
One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.

I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.

That’s about what I knew going into this.

Naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.)

So I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.

What followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (new Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.

From “it works” to 213 tokens per second

The chart follows the measured optimization sequence: 6 → 213 tokens/s, or 33× the baseline.

How much did the human advice help?

At one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.

Read the full FPGA design prompt

here is what someone else did for a dense bs=1 decode optimized fpga implementation for a dense qwen style model with ternary weights. you should take this with a grain of salt and pick things that you believe are acutally useful to add to your plan. Please also dont do things if you dont think is useful that take a lot of times like runnning really long test of a cycle accurate simulation etc or like physical design since those can take like hours. here are some ideas please pick and choose use this as context and not somehting that you shoudl be strictly guided by somethings that could help. prioritiize speed of like getting this up and running though..

MATMUL (TERNARY ENGINE) No multipliers. A 2-bit weight drives a 3:1 mux that picks x, ~x, or 0. The unused 4th code raises an error flag, so corrupt weights get caught. Negation is ~x + 1. Lanes flag negatives, and the row reducer adds the +1s once per row instead of once per lane. Activations are grouped integers: INT12, or INT16 where we needed more range (MLP down projection). Reduce as integers, apply FP32 group scales, accumulate in FP32. The pre-projection RMSNorm is deferred: quantize the activation first, apply the normalization scale after accumulation. It’s cheaper and numerically equivalent. 8 cores in two clusters. Projections that are independent (gate/up) run at the same time on separate core groups. Result: about half the DSPs of an INT8/INT16 design at the same rate, traded for more LUTs. MEMORY Weights are packed at 2 bits, 8x more per transfer than 16-bit. At batch 1, weight fetch costs far more energy and time than the math. Weights stream from HBM straight into the compute lanes and skip the on-chip buffers (they’re used once per token). Activations are cached next to each core and reused across rows. HBM routing is one chain per memory channel instead of a big crossbar. Lay out data so all 32 channels stay busy. On-chip buffers are typed slots with an explicit lifecycle (open -> write -> commit -> read -> release). Each slot has a side memory for scales/exponents. The buffer checks format, range and producer, which catches scheduling bugs in hardware. The KV cache is MXINT8: 8-bit values with one shared exponent per 32-channel block. That’s small enough to stream, with accuracy held. For MoE: stripe each expert across every channel, and map expert ID to address at runtime instead of using a fixed program. ATTENTION Attention streams over the cache in 64-token tiles with an online softmax (FP32 running max/sum). The full score matrix is never stored. Probabilities are UINT16 and the context accumulates in FP32. Each attention unit interleaves two independent jobs on one datapath (C-slow), which hides pipeline latency without duplicating hardware. Q/K head norm and RoPE got their own small vector unit, so they don’t block the general vector path. The V projection overlaps with that work. New K/V is appended to HBM as soon as it’s produced. We used a sliding window to bound cache reads. SCHEDULING One controller issues work in program order, with tags and barriers. Engines overlap only when the buffer dependencies are explicit, so we got overlap without races. For MoE: the router is the new critical path, because nothing can fetch until it finishes. Keep it in FP32 (lower precision changed which experts were picked), and overlap whatever you can around it. CORRECTNESS (maybe not neecessary to folow super close) We fixed a numerics contract first (formats, rounding points, operation order) and built hardware to match it. Vector ops must match the reference model’s order and precision, not just be “close”. Verification ladder: Per-block cocotb unit tests.One full layer co-simulated against the real checkpoint.Multi-token, full 24-layer decode compared token-for-token with a reference oracle.Byte-level accounting of KV cache writes. We kept simulation results, timing signoff and board results separate, and never claimed one from another. Every published number links to the report it came from. PHYSICAL DESIGN (maybe not necessary for u) The chip has 3 regions (SLRs). Keep wide datapaths inside one region and register every crossing. Long links use credits, not combinational ready. We placed engines next to their data: memory logic near HBM, attention in the DSP-dense region. Screen logic depth (10 levels max at 250 MHz) right after synthesis, and fix it with pipelining, sharding, or C-slow. Full place-and-route is saved for integration. Dev loop: small change -> lint -> unit test -> quick synthesis -> depth/timing check -> restructure.

The coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:

Read the agent’s retrospective: what it adopted and rejected

Its biggest design ideas were already in my plan before you pasted it. You pasted it on Oct 29 at 21:50 UTC: 4,741 characters describing what someone else did for a dense, batch-1, ternary FPGA decoder. Within 70 seconds I had sorted it into ten ideas to adopt and five to reject, and written that into every design agent’s brief. The shorter remark from your friend Edward, about using lookup tables as logic gates, came 24 minutes earlier and left nothing on the speed line.

Design ideas I adopted: mostly confirmation.

Already planned: streaming weights straight into the compute lanes, running rows in parallel, and reading the attention cache in bursts were all in the design brief I’d launched 35–40 minutes earlier.

 Match what was later built: interleaved lanes in the router (step 3);a separate unit for head norms and RoPE (step 4);a program-order sequencer (step 5);a registered boundary on every crossing between dies (steps 8 and 12). I can’t show these wouldn’t have happened without the notes.

Ideas I rejected: all five numerics shortcuts. Lower-precision activations, a deferred norm, an 8-bit KV cache, online softmax and 16-bit probabilities each change the output bits. That is where their design got its efficiency, and your bit-exact rule ruled it out.

Process advice: this changed things right away.

What you asked: not to do things that take hours.

What I stopped: a simulation that had run for about 24 hours, and two 250 MHz builds.

What I switched to: a short loop of C tests, synthesis and a logic-depth check, with one place-and-route per integration.

Likely gain: it got hardware results sooner.

Possible cost, which I can’t prove: two hangs that only RTL simulation could show reached the board the next day, and the big integration lost 38 hours to them.

One real find it triggered. While checking their memory ideas, I found AWS’s own reference memory design, which reaches 426 GB/s across all 32 memory channels. The memory subsystem was built from it.

In other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.

The optimization log

Here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.

0Baseline6.43 tok/s

Baseline: the first full-model bit-exact FPGA image (R8), served with host-side prefix caching.

1.0× from baseline

1Host overhead8.07 tok/s

Host software only: per-command overhead fell from ~10 ms to 0.9 ms (persistent register mapping, streaming reads, no per-command SDK calls or fsyncs).

1.25× this step · 1.25× from baseline

2Burst attention14.02 tok/s

A 128-lane attention engine that reads the KV cache in bursts instead of a word at a time, keeping the reference's exact summation order.

1.74× this step · 2.18× from baseline

3Parallel router20.53 tok/s

A parallel MoE router with an exact GCC-sort tie-breaker plus a streaming output head with built-in argmax; moderate-effort routing let it run at 250 MHz.

1.46× this step · 3.19× from baseline

4Glue engine30.24 tok/s

entry.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
entry.content:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:

First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.

All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.

What is the right code for this?

If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:

Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.

In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.

Why AI won’t push back

AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.

Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.

Your new job is to architect

AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:

Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.

That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.

If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.

Your future as developer

In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.
